title: Claims of biologics, and documented medical effects
notes: Kept although Appendix T expected it to be thin: Cash-Landrum and the AAWSAP medical work carry it past six.

lead.text: The board keeps two things apart: the claim that non-human biologics have been recovered, for which no material has been released, and a documented record of injuries attributed to encounters, chiefly the DIA-commissioned AAWSAP medical studies and the Cash-Landrum lawsuit, dismissed in 1986.

summary.text: The biologics claim has no released material; the medical record has DIRD 26 and the Cash-Landrum clinical record, which the board treats as the auditable end of the same question.

DIA's AAWSAP solicitation broke the work into twelve technical areas, one of them Human Effects of advanced technology on operators, and the contract's reference documents include a human-injury study, a survey of biosensors and BioMEMS, and three papers by Richard Genik of Wayne State.

On the board's inference, any sustained biological exploitation effort would need containment, pathology, genomics and tissue-banking infrastructure whose procurement and staffing could be audited independently of the material itself.

The board files plasma interpretations here: the Condon Report carries a chapter by Martin D. Altschuler on atmospheric electricity and plasma interpretations of UFOs, and the NASA study team named poor calibration and missing metadata as obstacles to telling atmospheric phenomena from anomalous objects.

record.text: DIRD 'Anomalous Acute and Subacute Field Effects on Human Biological Tissues', dated 11 March 2010 in the Acquisition Threat Support series, 38 pages, is in the DIA FOIA release with its author withheld. Its inside cover states it was produced in FY 2009 under DIA's Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program.

DIA's list sent to the Senate Armed Services Committee on 9 January 2018 names Dr Kit Green of Wayne State University as author of the same study, under the shorter title Field Effects on Biological Tissues.

A second document, the clinical DIRD written by Green and released publicly by Popular Mechanics on 14 February 2020, carries the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin imprint and states as Hypothesis One that "sufficient evidence exists from human injury / effects to reverse engineer certain aspects of the Energy / Propulsion Systems". Its preface quotes a November 2007 proposal addressed to Puthoff/Hathaway on 'Probable ET Generated Specific Near-field Electromagnetic Emissions'.

What the document asserts, in its own executive summary, is that reported incidents and acquired medical data "support a hypothesis that some advanced systems are already deployed, and opaque to full US Intelligence understanding". It draws on 42 peer-reviewed cases and about 300 unpublished ones, names the Cash-Landrum event, and proposes a continuation evaluating 300 to 500 events, with decisions on investigation taken together with its sponsors.

Wayne State's School of Medicine described Green as an adjunct professor and Fellow in Clinical Neuroimaging who had been executive director of its Emergent Technology Research Division. Richard Genik, the division's director, wrote three DIRDs, among them Cognitive Limits on Simultaneous Control of Multiple Unmanned Spacecraft, so Wayne State supplied four of the 38.
The DIRD Biosensors and BioMEMS, attributed on DIA's list to Dr Bruce Towe of the University of Arizona, surveys brain-implanted neuroelectrodes, implantable sensors and brain-machine interfaces.

Among the DIRDs the board files under plasma physics is Inertial Electrostatic Confinement Fusion, entry 1 on DIA's list, by Dr George Miley of the University of Illinois, one of four fusion-adjacent deliverables in the set.

Betty Cash, Vickie Landrum and Colby Landrum sued the United States in the Southern District of Texas, Civil Action No. H-84-348, under 28 U.S.C. 1346(b) and 2671 et seq., over the December 1980 encounter on FM 1485. Judge Ross N. Sterling dismissed the case on the government's motion by order filed 21 August 1986.

John Schuessler and Project VISIT taped a hospital interview in early February 1981, investigated on site on 28 February and filed a 35-page report with MUFON on 4 March 1981; he published the case file in 1998.

The Armed Forces Institute of Pathology was created in the Department of Defense by 10 U.S.C. 176 in 1976. The 2005 base-closure commission directed that all its elements be disestablished except the National Medical Museum and the Tissue Repository, and a 2008 statute required a Joint Pathology Center that maintains the Tissue Repository; 10 U.S.C. 176 remains in force.

The base-closure commission itself found the Department had failed to address several AFIP functions, such as the Radiologic Pathology program with its associated tissue repository, veterinary pathology and continuing medical education.

The UAP Disclosure Act's definitions reach biological evidence: a legacy program includes private-sector efforts to examine biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence, and a controlling authority includes any private entity in physical possession of such evidence.

claimed.text: David Grusch first made the biologics claim in his NewsNation interview with Ross Coulthart and repeated it under oath on 26 July 2023 when Rep. Nancy Mace asked. Asked whether the biologics were human or nonhuman, he answered: "Nonhuman, and that was the assessment of people with direct knowledge on the program I talked to that are currently still on the program." His information came from individuals he interviewed and referred to the Intelligence Community Inspector General.

Green says that at CIA's Office of Scientific Intelligence he was the officer to whom UFO and anomalous-phenomena reporting was routed, and he maintains a clinical case series of unexplained injuries he associates with the phenomenon, drawn largely from military and intelligence personnel. He described the DIRD as focused on forensically assessing accounts of injuries from claimed encounters.

Green's human-effects interest predates the federal contract: he is reported to have sat on the science advisory board of Bigelow's NIDS, which, on Bigelow's account, sent veterinarians to perform necropsies on reported animal mutilations at no cost to ranchers.

Garry Nolan says people representing the government and an aerospace corporation approached him about medical harm from supposed interactions with an anomalous craft. The board links this to Green's DIRD as the same research question, while recording that no document connects the two engagements.

Richard Doty said in August 2026 that he knew of autopsies on recovered bodies from people at the Armed Forces Institute of Pathology, naming 'Kate Green', whom the board identifies as Kit Green, then corrected himself in the same passage from saying Green did autopsies to saying he saw reports. No document opened names any individual at the Institute.
How the Cash-Landrum case reached the record: Vickie Landrum was directed to Schuessler after telephoning NASA about the incident, and his investigation is the source of the case file.

The board infers that commissioning a human-injury paper inside an aerospace weapons study means the sponsors already held a body of injury cases, and that DIRD 26 is the only one of the 38 whose subject is injury to human beings.

contested.text: AARO's Volume I report states it found no empirical evidence for claims of recovered extraterrestrial technology or associated material.
AARO, an interested office, documented at least eight approaches to him between June 2023 and January 2024 and concluded he had no intention of providing it information.

The United States denied that the object and the aircraft were its own, and the court dismissed the Cash suit. An Army Inspector General investigator, Lt. Col. George Sarran, found no evidence the helicopters belonged to the armed forces while calling Cash and Landrum credible, and no documents from a Defense investigation into whether the object was a military device have surfaced.

The plaintiffs' own attorney, Peter Gersten, later said the suit was a bluff brought in the hope of a quiet settlement of the medical expenses, and Schuessler found no radioactivity when he checked Cash's car with a Geiger counter in early 1981.

There is a gap in the record of DIRD 26's authorship: the DIA release withholds the author and the board holds that the release alone does not establish Green's authorship, though DIA's 2018 list to Congress names him. The printed title also adds the words Anomalous and Human to the title DIA gave Congress.

The board records rather than resolves a conventional reading of the injuries: dermal burn and neurological presentations attributed to encounters are also produced by directed-energy and radiofrequency exposure, and it infers such testing could look like reported UAP to an untrained observer.

questions: How do the two Green documents relate? DIRD 26 is DIA's release with the author withheld, while the clinical DIRD with the Austin imprint was released by Popular Mechanics; is one a version of the other?
What is in Green's clinical case series and the Green-Morris case files, and do the roughly 300 unpublished cases exist in a government-held database?
Who were the Sponsors and Affiliates referred to in the DIRD's executive summary, and was the continuation study of 300 to 500 events ever funded?
Did the Defense Department's investigation into whether the Cash-Landrum object was a military device produce any documents?
Do Betty Cash's medical records support radiation injury, or, as critics such as Brad Sparks, Gary Posner and Brian Dunning argue, alopecia areata and pre-existing illness?
Where was the Cash-Landrum encounter exactly? Critics say the location was never fixed.
Why does CIA's own 1997 history of its UFO role not name Green or describe any post-1970s portfolio?
Has any biological material ever been produced for independent examination, and would the tissue-repository and pathology infrastructure a programme needs show up in procurement records?
